concepts.name: Good pull requests and conventional commit messages

questions.prompt: On your `feature` branch you run `git rebase main`. What happens to your feature commits?

choices.text: Git adds one merge commit that joins `main` into `feature`
They are replayed on top of `main` as new commits with new hashes
They are moved onto `main`, and `main` now points at your last commit
They are squashed into one commit and pushed to the remote

questions.explanation: Rebase takes the changes introduced by each of your commits and reapplies them, one by one, on top of `main`. Each reapplied commit is a new commit with a new SHA, and the result is a linear history. Rebasing `feature` doesn't move `main`, doesn't squash unless you ask it to, and never pushes. Creating a merge commit is what `git merge` does.

questions.prompt: What is the "golden rule" of rebasing in the Pro Git book?

choices.text: Always rebase instead of merging, so the project history stays linear
Only rebase when you are sure it will not cause any merge conflicts
Never rebase a branch before it has been pushed to the shared remote repository
Don't rebase commits that exist outside your repo and others may build on

questions.explanation: Rebasing replaces commits with new ones. If others already have the old commits, they now have duplicates, and their work has to be merged again. So rebase your local work before you push, but never rebase what you've shared. Rebasing purely local commits is exactly the safe case.

questions.prompt: Compare merge and rebase as ways to bring `main`'s new commits into your feature branch. When would you use each?

model_answer.summary: Merge records a new merge commit and keeps the real, branching history; rebase replays your commits on top of `main` and gives a linear history. Rebase your own unpushed work; merge when the commits are already shared.
key_points: Merge makes a new commit with two parents and leaves existing commits untouched
Rebase rewrites your commits as new commits (new hashes) on top of the target, giving a linear history
Both end with the same final snapshot; only the history differs
Never rebase commits others have pulled; use merge for shared branches
A common workflow: rebase local work onto `main` before pushing or opening a PR

questions.explanation: Pro Git notes that the final snapshot is the same either way; it's only the history that differs. The choice is about the history you want to read later and about not rewriting commits that other people depend on.

questions.prompt: A merge stops with conflict markers in `api.py`. You edit the file to the correct content and delete the markers. How do you tell Git this file's conflict is resolved?
questions.explanation: Staging the file with `git add` marks it resolved; after all conflicted files are staged, `git commit` completes the merge. `git reset api.py` unstages the file, the opposite of what you want. `--amend` would rewrite the previous commit. Deleting files inside `.git` by hand can leave the repository in a broken state.

questions.prompt: Halfway through `git rebase main` you hit a messy conflict and want to give up and return your branch to exactly where it was. Which command?
questions.explanation: `git rebase --abort` stops the rebase and restores the branch to its state before the rebase began. `--skip` is the dangerous look-alike: it drops the commit that conflicted and carries on, so that commit's changes are lost from the result. `--continue` (for a rebase, `git rebase --continue`) is what you run after fixing and staging a conflict.

questions.prompt: You haven't pushed yet. Your last commit forgot a file. Which commands fix the commit without adding a new one or changing its message?

choices.text: `git add forgotten.py` then `git commit -m "add forgotten file"`

questions.explanation: `--amend` replaces the last commit with a new one that includes whatever is staged, and `--no-edit` keeps the old message. The amended commit gets a new SHA, so only do it before pushing. A plain `git commit` adds a second commit. `revert` creates a commit that undoes the last one. `reset --hard` throws away the commit and your uncommitted changes.

questions.prompt: You ran `git reset --hard HEAD~3` by mistake and your three latest commits vanished from `git log`. None were pushed. How do you get them back?

choices.text: You can't: `--hard` deletes the commits permanently
Run `git revert HEAD~3` to bring them back
Run `git pull`, since the remote still has them
Find the old tip in `git reflog`, then `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}`

questions.explanation: The commits still exist; nothing points at them any more. The reflog records every move of `HEAD`, so right after the reset, `HEAD@{0}` is the reset and `HEAD@{1}` is where `HEAD` was just before it. Resetting to `HEAD@{1}` restores the branch. The remote can't help with commits that were never pushed, and `revert` makes a new commit that undoes changes.

questions.prompt: You made two unrelated changes in the same file and want them in two separate commits. Which command lets you stage only some of the changes?
questions.explanation: `git add -p` (`--patch`) shows each hunk and asks whether to stage it: `y` yes, `n` no, `s` to split a hunk into smaller ones. Stage one change, commit, then stage the rest. `git add -A` and `git commit -a` take every change at once, and `git stash` puts all of them aside.

questions.prompt: Explain what the reflog is, how it can rescue you after a bad `reset`, `rebase` or `--amend`, and what its limits are.

model_answer.summary: The reflog is a local log of where `HEAD` and each branch tip have pointed. Commits you "lost" by moving a branch are usually still reachable through it, but it is local-only and its entries expire.
key_points: It records each time `HEAD` or a branch tip moved in your local repository
Old positions are named `HEAD@{n}`; `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` or `git branch rescue HEAD@{n}` gets a lost commit back
It works because reset, rebase and amend don't delete old commits straight away; they just stop pointing at them
It is local only: it isn't pushed, and a fresh clone has none of your history of moves
Entries expire (by default 90 days, or 30 for unreachable commits) and garbage collection can then delete the commits

questions.explanation: The `git reflog` manual describes it as a record of when branch tips and other references were updated in the local repository. The expiry defaults are `gc.reflogExpire` (90 days) and `gc.reflogExpireUnreachable` (30 days).

questions.prompt: Under Conventional Commits 1.0.0, which message marks a breaking change?
questions.explanation: A `!` after the type or scope, or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer, marks a breaking change, which maps to a MAJOR version bump. `fix` maps to PATCH and `feat` to MINOR. Other types such as `chore`, `docs` and `test` are allowed, but a scope or a word in the description doesn't signal a breaking change.

questions.prompt: What makes a good pull request? Describe how you would prepare one for a change that adds API-key authentication and a per-key rate limiter to your agent API.

model_answer.summary: A good PR is small and has one purpose, explains the problem, the approach and how it was tested, and has been reviewed by its author first. Here that means two PRs, auth first, then the rate limiter, each with tests.
key_points: Keep it small and focused on one purpose: split auth and rate limiting into separate PRs
Write a clear title and description: the problem, the approach, and anything reviewers should look at closely
Include tests and say how the change was tested (for example `TestClient` tests for 401 and 429 responses)
Review your own diff and check the builds and tests pass before asking for review
Use clear commit messages, such as `feat(auth): require an API key on /chat`

questions.explanation: GitHub's guidance is that small, focused pull requests are easier to review and safer to merge, that a clear description helps reviewers understand the problem, approach and result, and that authors should review their own PR first.
